draft.title: Biodiversity hotspots
card: A biodiversity hotspot is a region that is very rich in species and is also under severe threat. It is a way of deciding where conservation effort is most urgent.
species found in one region and nowhere else. A hotspot must have a very large number of them.
a hotspot must also have lost a large share of its original natural vegetation, mostly through human activity such as clearing land.
South-west Australia is a hotspot. It has many plants found nowhere else, and much of its native vegetation has been cleared for farming and towns.
draft.remember: A hotspot needs both: many endemic species and severe threat.

a.q: Which description best fits a biodiversity hotspot?
opts: Many endemic species and a large loss of natural vegetation
Many endemic species in a region with little human impact
Many species in total, all of which also live elsewhere
A large national park with strong legal protection
a.why: A hotspot combines high numbers of endemic species with severe threat. A region with many endemic species but little threat is not a hotspot, because the threat condition is missing.
a.clue: A hotspot must meet two conditions at once.

b.q: Region X has thousands of plant species, but nearly all also grow in neighbouring regions, and its forests are mostly intact. Why is Region X not a hotspot?
opts: It has few endemic species and is not severely threatened
It has few endemic species, though it is severely threatened
It has many endemic species and is not severely threatened
It has too many species for conservation to be urgent
b.why: Region X meets neither condition. Its species are found elsewhere, so it has few endemic species, and its forests are mostly intact, so it is not severely threatened. High species numbers alone do not make a hotspot.
b.clue: Check each of the two conditions against the region.

a.best: Many endemic species and a large loss of natural vegetation

b.best: It has few endemic species and is not severely threatened

problems.detail: The first bullet defines a hotspot as 'very rich in species', without saying the species must be found nowhere else. Question b then teaches that a region very rich in species is not a hotspot. The bullet should say 'very rich in endemic species' (species found nowhere else) to match the chapter point.
